    #Tutorial 2 (Potential Flow Theory)

    #Question 1

    Stream Function

    ∂y∂ψ​=u=2y

    ∫∂ψ=∫2y ∂y

    ψ=y2+f(x)

    ∂x∂ψ​=−v=−3x

    ∫∂ψ=∫−3x ∂x

    ψ=−23​x2+f(y)

    From observation,

    ∴ ψ=−23​x2+y2

    Vorticity

    ζ=ωz​=∂x∂v​−∂y∂u​

    ζ=3−2=1

    Since ζ=0, the flow is rotational.

    Let ψ=0.

    y2=23​x2 (in red)

    Let ψ=2.

    y2=23​x2+2 (in blue)

    Let ψ=−2.

    y2=23​x2−2 (in green)

    #Question 2

    Irrotational Flow

    ψ=3x2−3y2

    ∂y∂ψ​=u=−6y

    −∂x∂ψ​=v=−6x

    ζ=∂x∂v​−∂y∂u​

    ζ=−6−(−6)=0

    Since ζ=0, the flow is irrotational.

    Velocity Potential

    ∂x∂ϕ​=u=−6y

    ∫∂ϕ=∫−6y ∂x

    ϕ=−6xy+f(y)

    ∂y∂ϕ​=v=−6x

    ∫∂ϕ=∫−6x ∂y

    ϕ=−6xy+f(x)

    ∴ϕ=−6xy

    Prove for Orthogonal

    For a streamline, dψ=0.

    dψ=u dy−v dx=0

    dxdy​=uv​=∂ψ/∂y−∂ψ/∂x​

    dxdy​=−6y−6x​=yx​

    For a potential line, dϕ=0.

    dϕ=u dx+v dy=0

    dxdy​=−vu​=∂ϕ/∂y∂ϕ/∂x​

    dxdy​=−−6x−6y​=−xy​

    Since the gradient of the streamline is the negative reciprocal of the gradient of
    the potential line, streamlines and velocity potential lines are always orthogonal.

    #Question 3

    Combining the two flows,

    ϕ=ϕ1​+ϕ2​

    ϕ=3ln(r)+2x

    ϕ=3ln(r)+2rcosθ

    Vector r can be expressed in terms of x and y.

    Differentiating w.r.t. r​

    r1​∂θ∂ψ​=∂r∂ϕ​

    r1​∂θ∂ψ​=r3​+2cosθ

    ∂θ∂ψ​=3+2rcosθ

    Differentiating w.r.t. θ

    −∂r∂ψ​=r1​∂θ∂ϕ​

    −∂r∂ψ​=r1​(0−2rsinθ)

    ∂r∂ψ​=2sinθ

    Integrating the above,

    ∫∂ψ=∫3+2rcosθ ∂θ

    ψ=3θ+2rsinθ+f(r)

    Integrating the above,

    ∫∂ψ=∫2sinθ ∂r

    ψ=2rsinθ+f(θ)

    By observation,

    ψ=3θ+2rsinθ

    ψ=3tan−1xy​+2y

    #Question 4

    The flow around a circular cross-section cable
    can be described by a doublet in uniform flow.

    Stream function is then,

    ψ=Ursinθ(1−r2a2​)

    Differentiating to get vr​ and vθ​,

    vr​=r1​∂θ∂ψ​=Ucosθ(1−r2a2​)

    vθ​=−∂r∂ψ​=−Usinθ(1+r2a2​)

    The boundary of the Rankine oval is where r=a.

    vr​=0

    vθ​=−2Usinθ

    There is only tangential velocity on the surface of the cable.

    Using Bernoulli’s equation,

    whereby subscript a denotes an arbitrary point on the boundary
    and     pa​ is the static pressure at that point of interest

    p0​+21​ρU2=pa​+21​ρUa​2

    pa​=p0​+21​ρU2−21​ρUa​2

    pa​=p0​+21​ρ[U2−(−2Usinθ)2]

    pa​=p0​+21​ρ(U2−4U2sin2θ)

    pa​=p0​+21​ρU2(1−4sin2θ)

    To achieve maximum static pressure, 1−4sin2θ≥0, thus sinθ=0.

    Location of maximum static pressure occurs at 0° and 180°.

    pmax​=p0​+21​ρU2

    To achieve minimum static pressure, 1−4sin2θ<0, thus sinθ=1.

    Location of minimum static pressure occurs at 90°.

    pmin​=p0​+21​ρU2(1−4)

    pmin​=p0​−23​ρU2

    Substituting θ=4π​ and r=2a into the stream function,

    ψ=U(2a)sin4π​(1−4a2a2​)

    ψ=U⋅2a⋅22​​⋅43​

    ψ=43Ua⋅2​​

    ψ=22​3Ua​

    #Question 5

    The slit can be approximated as a half-sink.

    The continuity equation for a half sink is,

    −Q=21​(2πr)vr​

    −Q=πr⋅vr​

    vr​=−πrQ​

    There is only flow in the 0≤θ≤180° range.

    The flow over the flat surface can be approximated as a uniform flow. At some
    distance a from the sink, velocity due to the sink must be equal in magnitude
    to velocity U of the uniform flow, at which a stagnation point will form.

    vr​=U

    πaQ​=U

    a=πUQ​

    a=2π0.05​

    a=0.0079577 m=7.96 mm

    Since a sink only has radial velocity, magnitude of the velocity due to sink is simply vr​.

    Air is sucked into the slit at a flow rate of 0.05 m3/s per unit length into the paper. Thus, the red shaded region consists of
    the air being sucked into the slit.

    Let unit length into the paper be 1 m.

    Q⋅1=AU=(h⋅1)U

    h=UQ​=20.05​=0.025 m=25 mm

    #Question 6

    #Part (a)

    Q=(2πr)vr​

    vr​=2πrQ​

    Resolving the velocity vector vr​,

    u=vr​cosθ=2πrQcosθ​

    v=vr​sinθ=2πrQsinθ​

    #Part (b)

    At some point along the x-axis, velocity due to the
    source will cancel out the velocity of the uniform flow.

    For a source, there is only radial velocity vr​.

    vr​=2πrQ​

    At some radius b from the source, the velocity is equal in magnitude to the velocity U of the uniform flow, but opposite in direction. Hence, net velocity at this point is zero.

    U=2πbQ​

    b=2πUQ​

    #Part (c)

    The stream function of the Rankine half-body is,

    ψ=Ursinθ+2πQ​⋅θ

    The boundary of the half-body passes through the stagnation point.
    Thus, the stream function of this boundary is when r=b and θ=π.

    The angle θ is measured anticlockwise from the x-axis.

    Substituting r=b and θ=π into ψ,

    ψstagnation​=Ub⋅sinπ+2Q​

    ψstagnation​=2Q​

    ψstagnation​=πbU

    Substituting the above back into ψ and expressing 2πQ​ in terms of b,

    πbU=Ursinθ+2πQ​⋅θ

    πbU=Ursinθ+bU⋅θ

    r=sinθb(π−θ)​

    where r is the radial distance from the source in
    which a point lies on the stagnation streamline

    Since y=rsinθ,

    y=b(π−θ)

    As x→∞, the angle θ→0.

    The vector r becomes nearly parallel to the x-axis.

    y=bπ

    #Part (d)

    Flow Half-Width

    The stream function that P lies on is,

    Since P lies on the y-axis, θ=2π​.

    ψp​=Uyp​+2πQ​(2π​)

    ψp​=Uyp​+4Q​

    Since P lies on the half-body surface, which is the stagnation streamline,

    ψp​=ψstagnation​

    2Q​=Uyp​+4Q​

    yp​=4UQ​

    Flow Velocity and Direction

    At P where θ=2π​,

    rp​=sin(π/2)b(π−π/2)​

    rp​=2bπ​

    rp​=4UQ​

    Velocity components consists of velocity due to
    the uniform flow and velocity due to the source.

    u=U+vr​cosθ=U+2πrQcosθ​

    v=vr​sinθ=2πrQsinθ​

    Substituting rp​=4UQ​ and θ=2π​,

    u=U

    v=π2U​

    Vp​=u2+v2​

    Vp​=U2+π24U2​​

    Vp​=U1+π24​​

    Flow Direction=tan−1(U2U/π​)

    Flow Direction=tan−1π2​

    Flow Direction=32.482°

    #Question 4

    z=4t⋅cx​(1−cx​)

    z=4tcx​−4tc2x2​

    Differentiating and using variable transformation,

    dxdz​=c4t​−8tc2x​

    dxdz​=c4t​−c4t​(1−cosθ)

    dxdz​=c4t​cosθ

    0≤cx​≤1

    0≤1−cosθ≤2

    1≥cosθ≥−1

    0≤θ≤π

    #Part (a)

    A0​=α−π1​∫0π​dxdz​ dθ

    A0​=α−πc4t​∫0π​cosθ dθ

    A0​=α−πc4t​[sinθ]0π​

    A0​=α

    A1​=π2​∫0π​dxdz​cosθ dθ

    A1​=π2​∫0π​c4t​cos2θ dθ

    A1​=πc8t​∫0π​21​(cos2θ+1) dθ

    A1​=πc4t​[sin2θ+θ]0π​

    A1​=πc4t​⋅π

    A1​=c4t​

    A2​=π2​∫0π​dxdz​cos2θ dθ

    A2​=π2​∫0π​c4t​cosθcos2θ dθ

    A2​=πc8t​∫0π​cosθ(2cos2θ−1) dθ

    A2​=πc8t​∫0π​2cos3θ−cosθ dθ

    A2​=πc8t​[32​sinθ(cos2θ+2)−sinθ]0π​

    A2​=0

    #Part (b)

    Cl​=π(2A0​+A1​)

    Cl​=π(2α+c4t​)

    L′=21​ρ∞​U∞​2⋅c⋅Cl​

    L′=21​ρU2cπ(2α+c4t​)

    L′=ρU2π(αc+2t)

    where L′ is lift per unit span

    #Part (c)

    CmLE​​=−2π​(A0​+A1​−2A2​​)

    CmLE​​=−2π​(α+c4t​)

    MLE′​=21​ρ∞​U∞​2c2⋅CmLE​​

    MLE′​=21​ρU2c2⋅−2π​(α+c4t​)

    #Question 4

    #Part (a)

    Assume infinite wing uses a symmetrical airfoil.
    Thus, zero-lift angle of attack is αL=0​=0°.

    Lift curve slope of the infinite wing is then,

    dαdCL​​=α−αL=0​CL​−CL0​​​

    dαdCL​​=4°(π/180)1​

    dαdCL​​=14.324/rad

    Lift curve slope of infinite wing accounted for downwash effect.

    Span effectiveness factor of finite wing,

    e=1+0.041​=0.96154

    Lift curve slope of the finite wing is then,

    dαdCL​​=1+πeARa0​​a0​​

    dαdCL​​=1+π(0.96154)(7.5)14.324​14.324​

    dαdCL​​=8.7756/rad

    Lift curve slope of finite wing accounted for downwash effect.

    Angle of attack is,

    dαdCL​​=αCL​​

    α=8.77561​

    α=0.11395 rad=6.5290°

    #Part (b)

    From Part (a), dαdCL​​=14.324/rad and e=0.96154.

    Lift curve slope of the finite wing is then,

    dαdCL​​=1+π(0.96154)(6)14.324​14.324​

    dαdCL​​=8.0141/rad

    Angle of attack is,

    dαdCL​​=αCL​​

    α=8.01411​

    α=0.12478 rad=7.1494°

    #Part (c)

    A decrease in AR results in an increase in α required to achieve the same CL​.
    Since αi​=πeARCL​​, a decrease in AR results in an increase in induced αi​,
    while effective αeff​ remains the same so as to generate the same CL​.
    Thus, the geometric α increases overall.

    #Question 3

    Cp0​​=−0.41

    Pressure coefficient under incompressible flow conditions.

    Cp​=1−M∞​2​−0.41​

    Cpcr​​=1−Mcr​2​−0.41​

    Predicted pressure coefficient under compressible flow conditions.

    Since Cp0​​ is the minimum pressure coefficient, Cp​ would also be the
    minimum pressure coefficient in a compressible flow. Thus, at the
    point of minimum pressure, when M∞​=Mcr​, then Cp​=Cpcr​​.

    Cpcr​​=γMcr​22​{[1+21​(γ−1)1+21​(γ−1)Mcr​2​]γ−1γ​−1}

    1−Mcr​2​−0.41​=γMcr​22​{[1+21​(γ−1)1+21​(γ−1)Mcr​2​]γ−1γ​−1}

    1−Mcr​2​−0.41​=1.4Mcr​22​{[1.21+0.2Mcr​2​]3.5−1}

    Mach NumberLeft-Hand SideRight-Hand Side
    0.72-0.6196-0.6996
    0.73-0.6292-0.6621
    0.74-0.6393-0.6260
    0.737-0.6362-0.6367
    0.7371-0.6363-0.6363

    By subsituting values of Mcr​, through trial-and-error, when the left-hand side is
    equal to the right-hand side of the equation, the Mach number is then the Mcr​.

    #Question 4

    #Method 1

    Since M∞​=Mcr​=0.8, the flow speed at minimum pressure point is M=1.

    CpA​​=γM∞​22​{[1+21​(γ−1)MA​21+21​(γ−1)M∞​2​]γ−1γ​−1}

    where A is the minimum pressure point

    Pressure coefficient at A is,

    Cp​=1.4(0.8)22​{[1+21​(1.4−1)(1)21+21​(1.4−1)(0.8)2​]0.41.4​−1}

    Cp​=−0.43464

    Using the alternative expression for Cp​,

    Cp​=γM∞​22​(p∞​p​−1)

    −0.43464=1.4(0.8)22​(p∞​p​−1)

    p∞​p​=0.80528

    #Method 2

    p∞​pA​​=p0​pA​​⋅p∞​p0​​

    where A is the minimum pressure point

    From isentropic flow properties table, at MA​=1,

    pA​p0​​=1.893

    p0​pA​​=0.52826

    From isentropic flow properties table, at M∞​=0.8,

    p∞​p0​​=1.524

    Pressure ratio at A is then,

    p∞​pA​​=0.52826(1.524)

    p∞​pA​​=0.80507

    #Question 5

    At slightly below transonic speed M<0.8:

    • Flow above and below the airfoil accelerates to slightly below M1
    • No shockwaves form and thus, no flow separation due to shockwaves occur
    • Wake produced by the airfoil is small and thus, drag of the airfoil is low

    As speed increases to critical Mach number Mcr​:

    • Shockwave forms near the trailing edge of the airfoil on the upper surface
    • Flow separation occurs directly downstream of the shockwave
    • Wake produced by the airfoil increases in size
    • Drag of the airfoil increases due to wake drag

    As speed increases further from Mcr​ to Mdd​:

    • Another shockwave forms near the trailing edge on the lower surface
    • Shockwave on the upper surface shifts backwards toward the trailing edge
    • Flow separation occurs on both the upper and lower surfaces of the airfoil
    • Drag of the airfoil drastically increases beyond Mdd​

    As speed increases from Mdd​ to M1:

    • Both shockwaves shift toward the trailing edge of the airfoil
    • Flow is supersonic both above and below the airfoil
    • Wake produced by the airfoil becomes smaller in size

    At speeds beyond M1:

    • A bow shockwave forms at the leading edge of the airfoil
    • Bow shockwave eventually attaches itself to leading edge at higher Mach numbers

    #Tutorial 8 (Experimental Aerodynamics)

    #Question 1

    #Part (a)

    Particle image velocimetry:

    • Tracer particles (smoke/oil droplets) are released into airflow
    • Laser light source creates a thin light sheet that illuminates the particles
    • High speed camera/s record the motion of the suspended particles
    • Time interval between two images used to determine particle velocity
    • Velocity vectors of every particle gives the velocity field of the flow

    Able to achieve:

    • Generates global measurement results of the vortex core
    • Location and dissipation of vortex core can be tracked
    • Vorticity of fluid can be determined from velocity measurements
    • Allows for comparison of the vortex strength of each wing tip design

    Potential pitfall:

    • Non-uniform particle distribution within vortex core due to centrifugal force

    #Part (b)

    Issues with pressure measurements:

    • Large number of PVC tubing may be required
    • Air in tubing leads to resonance at certain frequencies
    • Size of tubing results in signal amplification/attenuation
    • Measured pressures will deviate from actual pressures

    Tubing frequency response correction method:

    • Each PVC tubing is calibrated against a short reference tubing
    • Frequency response of tubing is obtained as a Fourier series
    • Apply correction factors on coefficients of Fourier series
    • Perform an inverse Fourier transformation
    • Setup consists of a speaker driven at a known frequency and amplitude
    • Frequency response of PVC tubing and reference tubing are measured

    #Part (c)

    Laser doppler anemometry:

    • Non-intrusive measurement technique — does not disturb the vortex core
    • Hot wire is fragile and will most likely break when placed in the turbulent flow

    #Question 2

    #Part (a)

    Pressure sensitive paint:

    • Global pressure measurement
    • Responds to pressure fluctuations
    • Accurate if calibrated properly (pressure-luminence relationship is established)
    • The higher the test speed, the greater the variation in paint color

    #Part (b)

    Particle image velocimetry:

    • Fast experiment
    • Global velocity field measurement
    • Other variables can be derived from velocity measurements
    • Simple calibration for 2D measurements

    #Question 3

    #Part (a)

    Causes of horizontal stabilizer fluttering:

    • Flow separation from main wings
    • Formation of vortices at main wing root or leading edge extensions (LEX)
    • Vortices then impinge on the horizontal stabilizer which leads to fluttering
    • If vortex frequency coincides with natrual frequency of stabilizer, flutter occurs

    #Part (b)

    Laser doppler anemometry:

    • Two laser beams of different frequencies are used to create intersection volume
    • An inteference pattern is formed within the intersection volume
    • Tracer particles (microspheres, etc) are introduced into the flow
    • Particles scatter the laser light as it passes through the volume
    • Scattering of light results in a frequency shift (Doppler effect)
    • Frequency shift is proportional to particles’ velocity
    • An optic is used to detect the Doppler shift

    Advantages:

    • Robust
    • No calibration required
    • High frequency response
    • Non-intrusive (does not require a probe to be placed in the flow)

    Disadvantages:

    • Relatively expensive
    • Requires more setup preparation
    • Requires tracer particles
    • Requires optical access
    • Not feasible for curved surfaces

    #Part (c)

    Particle image velocimetry:

    • Fluid is seeded with small, neutrally buoyant particles (smoke)
    • Laser light source creates a thin light sheet that illuminates the particles
    • High-speed camera records the motion of the suspended particles
    • Time interval between two images gives the particle velocity
    • Velocity vectors of particles gives the velocity field of the flow

    Advantages:

    • Fast experiment
    • Non-intrusive
    • Global velocity field measurement
    • Other variables can be derived from velocity measurements

    Disadvantages:

    • Low frequency response
    • Significant post-processing time
    • Large datasets results in high storage requirement
    • Each vector is an average over a square cross-correlation window

    #Question 4

    #Part (a)

    Laser-induced fluorescence:

    • Release smoke into the airstream
    • Use a laser beam to create a thin laser sheet
    • Align laser sheet along visualization plane

    Justifications:

    • Simple and low-cost
    • Only the illuminated plane will be visualized

    #Part (b)

    Particle image velocimetry:

    • Fluid is seeded with small, neutrally buoyant particles (smoke)
    • Laser light source creates a thin light sheet that illuminates the particles
    • High-speed camera records the motion of the suspended particles
    • Time interval between two images gives the particle velocity
    • Velocity vectors of particles gives the velocity field of the flow

    Justifications:

    • Fast experiment
    • Non-intrusive
    • Global velocity field measurement
    • Freesteram velocity is subsonic with no shockwaves
    • Other variables can be derived from velocity measurements

    #Part (c)

    Modification to experiment:

    • Load cell or force transducer is attached to the base of the cylinder
    • Measurements are acquired by a data-acqusition card
    • Fast Fourier Transform analysis is performed on data
    • FFT reveals the peak frequency associated with vortex shedding

    #Part (d)

    To avoid aliasing effect, a high sampling frequency should be used. Only
    frequencies below the Nyquist frequency can be measured correctly.

    #Question 5

    #Part (a)

    Particle image velocimetry:

    • Fluid is seeded with small, neutrally buoyant particles (smoke)
    • Laser light source creates a thin light sheet that illuminates the particles
    • High-speed camera records the motion of the suspended particles
    • Time interval between two images gives the particle velocity
    • Velocity vectors of particles gives the velocity field of the flow
    • Vorticity can be estimated from the velocity field

    Justifications:

    • Global velocity measurement
    • Strength of blade tip vortices can be estimated

    #Part (b)

    At 1500 RPM,

    Vtan​=rω

    Vtan​=0.5⋅601500(2π)​

    Vtan​=78.5 m/s

    Vtip​=V∞​+Vtan​

    Vtip​=78.5+80

    Vtip​=158.5 m/s

    Since blade tip velocity is greater than 100 m/s, the flow experiences
    significant compressiblity effects, with the possibility of shockwaves.

    Schlieren photography:

    • Visualize shocks at blade tips and their interactions with tip vortex
    • Position region of interest between a white background and light source
    • Camera is placed behind white background to capture the shockwaves
    • Shockwaves will appear as dark/bright regions
